summary: Proposes TCP Port Service Multiplexer (TCPMUX), a way for future TCP services to be reached by name through one port instead of each getting its own well-known port. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of giving every shop its own street number, there is one front desk that sends you to the right shop when you say its name.

questions: how does the tcp port service multiplexer work
subtitle: A single TCP port that routes client requests to different services by name.

tldr.problem: Each TCP service needs its own well-known port number, but port numbers are a limited resource and assignment is slow.
tldr.mechanism: TCPMUX on port 1 receives the service name in text and replies with a positive or negative confirmation. If positive, the requested protocol begins; if negative, the connection closes.
tldr.outcome: The idea was not widely adopted, and the RFC became historic when replaced by RFC 7805.

today: RFC 1078 is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805. TCPMUX was not widely deployed, and modern protocols typically either use dedicated ports or negotiate over HTTP.

sections.title: The Port Shortage
sections.content: Well-known TCP ports are assigned for standard services and are limited in number. TCPMUX proposes a solution: use a single well-known port (port 1) to contact multiple services by name instead of assigning each service a unique port. This allows future services and private protocols to be accessed without requesting official port assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: Port numbers are scarce. This idea lets one port handle many services if you tell it the service name.

sections.title: How TCPMUX Works
sections.content: A client connects to port 1 on a remote host and sends the service name followed by carriage return and line feed. The server replies with a single character: "+" for success or "-" for failure, optionally followed by an explanation message and a line feed. If the reply is positive, the requested protocol begins. If negative, the connection closes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says the service name, the server says yes or no, and if yes, the real conversation starts.

sections.title: Service Names and Conventions
sections.content: The reserved name "HELP" instructs the server to list all supported services, one per line. Service names are case-insensitive. Standard services defined in RFC 1010 are reserved to their published definitions. Private services should use names prefixed with the organization's name to avoid conflicts. Multiple versions of a protocol can suffix the name with a version number.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can ask for "HELP" to see what services are available. Unofficial services should use unique names to avoid confusion.

sections.title: Negative and Positive Replies
sections.content: When TCPMUX cannot find a requested service, it sends a negative reply ("-") from the port-multiplexing process. When the requested service is found and can handle the connection, a positive reply ("+") comes from the service process itself. The character is sent immediately, optionally followed by an explanation message and a line feed.
sections.plainLanguage: The server answers quickly with yes or no. If yes, the real conversation starts. If no, the connection closes.

references.text: Reynolds, J. and J. Postel, "Assigned Numbers", RFC 1010, May 1987.
